query: Give official links and 150 words on S3 prefix IAM restrictions and DNS-01 challenge least-privilege credentials. Why test actual provider behavior?

content.text:
S3 and DNS-01 automation should both use narrowly scoped, short-lived credentials wherever the provider allows it. The key point is that policy syntax is only an intended boundary; the real API and provider implementation determine the effective boundary.

## Official links

- AWS: — IAM supports identity- and resource-based policies, and S3 access can be scoped to buckets, objects, and prefixes.
- AWS: — recommends least privilege and IAM roles with temporary credentials rather than embedded long-term access keys.
- AWS: — recommends deriving fine-grained policies from actual CloudTrail activity and testing them before production use.
- Let’s Encrypt: — describes publishing the _acme-challenge TXT record and explicitly warns against placing broad DNS API credentials on web servers.
- Certbot: — documents DNS plugins and _acme-challenge CNAME delegation as an option when the normal DNS provider is unsuitable for automated DNS-01.

## ~150 words

For S3, restrict object operations with resource ARNs such as arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/tenant-a/*; separately constrain s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN using s3:prefix, because listing targets the bucket rather than object ARNs. Avoid broad s3:*, bucket-wide object access, and permanent user keys; prefer workload IAM roles and temporary credentials. For DNS-01, the ACME client needs only the ability to create, read if required, and delete the validation TXT record at _acme-challenge.example.com—not general control of every DNS record, registrar settings, or every hosted zone. If the DNS provider cannot scope a token that tightly, delegate _acme-challenge to a dedicated zone/provider and issue credentials only there. Test actual provider behavior because IAM/DNS policy language, plugin requests, API quirks, inherited permissions, zone-discovery calls, credential scopes, and propagation behavior can differ from assumptions. A policy simulator helps, but end-to-end tests with a nonproduction name prove both positive access and expected denial paths. Let’s Encrypt specifically warns that full DNS API credentials on a web server greatly increase compromise impact.

## Practical validation

Test both the allowed and forbidden paths:
- S3: PutObject, GetObject, DeleteObject, and ListBucket inside the permitted prefix; then try sibling prefixes, bucket-wide listing, bucket policy changes, ACL changes, and unrelated buckets.
- DNS: run a staging ACME issuance/renewal against a delegated test name; ensure the credential can alter only the intended _acme-challenge record or dedicated validation zone, and cannot modify A, MX, NS, or other production zones.
- Observe the client/plugin’s exact calls. Some DNS integrations require zone enumeration or record lookup in addition to TXT writes, so a theoretically minimal credential may fail while a slightly broader—but still isolated—validation-zone token succeeds.
- Make denial tests part of CI or a periodic security check. AWS recommends using observed access activity to refine policies, then testing generated fine-grained policies before deployment.

Sources:
1. [How Amazon S3 works with IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security_iam_service-with-iam.html)
2. [S3 security best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security-best-practices.html)
3. [IAM least-privilege best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)
4. [Challenge types / DNS-01](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/challenge-types/)
5. [FAQ](https://certbot.eff.org/faq)
